summary:
Bhutan decriminalised consensual same-sex intimacy in 2021. The Penal Code Amendment Act entered into force on 17 February 2021, removing Sections 213 and 214, the 'unnatural sex' provisions that carried one month to one year of imprisonment and had gone unenforced for at least 15 years. The lower house voted 43-1 for repeal in June 2019; the upper house reinserted the ban; a December 2020 joint sitting resolved that homosexuality between adults shall not be considered unnatural sex. No reversal has followed.

The repeal created no protective framework. Bhutan has no stand-alone anti-discrimination law and no explicit protections on the grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, or sex characteristics. LGBTIQ organisations may register, though activists describe the process as lengthy and burdensome.

Legal gender recognition is unavailable. Administrative changes to a gender marker are suspended for lack of standardised guidelines; the pathway documented in official material requires a transgender applicant to submit a medical note together with a supporting letter from a civil society organisation.

Enforcement does not match the formal legal position. Bhutan Broadcasting Service reported in November 2024 that trans people are more than four times as likely to experience assault as the general population. A 49-year-old trans woman described having nowhere to report violence: police dismissed her complaints on the ground that her identity card records a male marker, treating the matter as violence between two men. Families press victims to accept the outcome as fate, and referrals routed through the LGBTQIA+ committee move slowly. The practical result is impunity for anti-trans violence.

Discrimination and stigma persist, with health-care access singled out as a setting where trans and LGBTIQ people are turned away or poorly served. Official guidance cuts the other way: the Bhutan Medical and Health Council's Code of Professional Fidelity, issued in 2021, protects sexual orientation, and the 2020 Standard Operating Procedure for Gender Based Violence Prevention and Response requires providers to deliver age-appropriate, culturally sensitive and sexual-orientation- and gender-identity-sensitive care, with case managers giving tailored support to people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities.

No form of legal recognition exists for same-sex relationships. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under Bhutanese law cannot have a partner recognised in any legal proceeding. A marriage bill drafted with gender-neutral pronouns was discussed in the 2018 summer parliamentary session but deferred because of that year's election; the community expected the conversation to resume under the incoming government, and no sourced outcome has followed.
tangentialFactors:
Bhutan's repeal lowered the count of states criminalising consensual same-sex intimacy from 72 to 71.

The 2024 Free & Equal campaign trained the Royal Court of Justice, the Attorney General's Office and the Cabinet Secretariat, and produced the first direct dialogue between Bhutan's LGBTIQ+ community and parliamentarians. Two consultation workshops brought community members together with UN and National Commission for Women and Children representatives.

Social invisibility, rather than open persecution, has been the documented pattern. A 2015 account reported that LGBT people described very little persecution or violence but near-total invisibility, with no shared vocabulary for gay or trans identities and lesbianism largely unrecognised. The LGBT Bhutan Facebook page, founded in 2013, produced the country's first public affirmation of a gay population.

Public trans visibility exists but remains exceptional. One of only two trans women living publicly in the country fought at 16 for the right to wear the female school uniform, the kira, a first in Bhutanese society.
localsOnly:
Rainbow Bhutan's director states that most LGBTQ youths drop out of school. Of the 316 people registered as LGBTQ in 2019, 10 were below the age of 19.

The National Strategic Framework on Comprehensive Sexuality Education (2021) covers LGBTI issues.
outOfScopeNotes:
Official material describes a gender-marker change pathway requiring a medical note and a civil society supporting letter, while other reporting states that administrative marker changes are suspended for want of standardised guidelines. Which procedure is currently operative is unresolved.

The November 2024 figure that trans people are more than four times as likely to experience assault is reported without the underlying survey basis or comparison data, so the precision of the multiplier cannot be verified.

Whether the 2018 gender-neutral marriage bill will be revived has no sourced outcome.
